primary_cause: Violent repricing of bank earnings and credit risk after Fed emergency zero-rate move. No meaningful Goldman-specific negative
secondary_factors: Recession fears. Liquidity stress. Broad forced deleveraging in financials
store_description: No meaningful Goldman-specific negative announcement in the prior 3 days. The Fed March 15 emergency action pushed rates to 0-0.25% and told investors the economy was deteriorating fast which is especially bad for banks spread income and credit outlook.

primary_cause: Anticipation of sharp COVID-driven advertising slowdown. No clear Alphabet-specific negative filing Mar 13-16
secondary_factors: Broad tech multiple compression. Fed-panic interpretation. Marketwide liquidation. Later Reuters confirmed Google search ad revenue fell mid-teens percentage in late March
store_description: Investors rapidly repriced Google ad business as the U.S. emergency declaration border restrictions and shutdowns hit advertiser demand. Reuters later showed Google search ads were down by a mid-teens percentage in late March.

primary_cause: Anticipated collapse in digital ad demand from COVID shutdowns. Same setup as GOOGL
secondary_factors: Nasdaq-wide de-risking. March 16 circuit-breaker session. Large advertisers in travel local commerce events and brand marketing pulling back
store_description: There was no separate GOOG-specific catalyst from GOOGL. The stock was likely hit by the same thesis: large advertisers in travel local commerce events and brand marketing were pulling back fast.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Reuters: GM drew down B revolving credit line suspended 2020 outlook faced plant shutdowns after employees tested positive. J.D. Power: U.S. new-vehicle demand fell 13% in first 19 days of March
secondary_factors: Recession risk. Credit-market stress. Cyclicals getting crushed in March 16 panic
store_description: Investors were staring at a double hit: collapsing demand and disrupted manufacturing. Reuters said GM pulled its 2020 outlook tapped B of credit and was shutting North American plants after positive virus cases while U.S. vehicle demand was already down 13%.

primary_cause: Market repricing of GE aviation and industrial cash-flow risk under COVID. Highly exposed to aviation and industrial end markets imploding
secondary_factors: High leverage concerns. Airline collapse. Severe industrial cyclicals de-risking. Reuters later quantified ~B industrial cash-flow hit from pandemic in Q1
store_description: GE was one of the names most vulnerable to investors worst-case COVID scenario. The market was effectively pricing in a major collapse in aviation demand and weaker industrial cash generation.

primary_cause: No major IBM-specific Reuters earnings or guidance shock. Broad enterprise IT and consulting demand fears tied to fast-moving recession
secondary_factors: General liquidation in large-cap tech and services. Lower investor appetite for legacy IT names in crisis. Already withdrawn from RSA in February
store_description: This looks more macro and demand-driven than IBM-idiosyncratic. As governments and companies froze travel and shifted into emergency mode investors likely marked down IBM consulting infrastructure and enterprise-spending exposure.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. FedEx suspended FY2020 profit outlook citing significant impact of coronavirus and ongoing TNT turnaround pressure. Reuters story filed late Mar 17
secondary_factors: Economic shutdown fears. Air-cargo disruption. General cyclical selling. Guidance suspension and uncertainty around shipment mix and global logistics
store_description: The stock March 16 weakness makes sense as anticipation ahead of earnings and the market was vindicated almost immediately when Reuters reported FedEx suspended its 2020 profit outlook. The company explicitly cited the significant coronavirus impact.

primary_cause: No Emerson-specific Mar 13-16 catalyst. Industrial recession fears especially tied to energy and capex
secondary_factors: Oil collapse. Broad liquidation in multi-industry names. Meaningful exposure to industrial capex energy and process automation
store_description: Emerson move looks mainly like a sector repricing rather than a company event. With oil having already crashed about 25% on March 9 and shutdowns spreading globally investors likely marked down demand for automation and process-equipment spending.

primary_cause: No Duke-specific announcement. Fed emergency actions interpreted as sign of severe economic damage. Forced liquidation and recession fears overriding utilities defensive status
secondary_factors: Fear of lower commercial and industrial electricity demand. Generalized dash-for-cash behavior
store_description: Duke drop was unusually large for a utility suggesting this was less about a company-specific problem and more about indiscriminate selling. The combination of the zero-rate emergency move circuit-breaker open and concern that business closures would dent commercial and industrial load.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Reuters Mar 12 reported Disney would close California and Florida parks and Paris resort through month-end. Theme-park closures and travel and entertainment shutdowns
secondary_factors: Film-release disruption. Cruise and travel weakness. Broad travel-service retrenchment
store_description: This was a very real Disney-specific earnings shock. The parks business is a huge cash generator and Reuters reported Disney was shutting the U.S. and Paris parks from that weekend through the end of the month.

primary_cause: Severe compression in high-multiple software names during March 16 panic. Salesforce announced Mar 13 event updates. Mar 16 said offices in North America and EMEA would move to hard close through at least Apr 15
secondary_factors: Event cancellations. Enterprise-spending fears. Risk-off rotation out of richly valued SaaS
store_description: Salesforce did have COVID-related operational news but it was not obviously negative enough by itself to justify a near-16% drop. The more likely driver was that the stock was a high-multiple enterprise software name being aggressively de-risked.

primary_cause: No negative Danaher-specific item. Cepheid unit would receive EUA for rapid SARS-CoV-2 test Mar 21. Broad market selloff before COVID-testing upside materialized
secondary_factors: Healthcare equipment de-risking. Cash-raising liquidation. Fear industrial and life-sciences demand would weaken
store_description: Danaher was caught in the indiscriminate March 16 selloff despite eventually becoming a COVID-testing beneficiary through Cepheid. Because the positive test catalyst had not yet arrived investors were probably still focused on recession risk.

primary_cause: No Deere-specific negative Mar 13-16. Reuters later reported Deere withdrew 2020 financial outlook Mar 23. Anticipation of deep global industrial and farm-equipment slowdown
secondary_factors: Dealer disruption. Financing stress. Recession-driven capex cuts
store_description: Deere traded like a classic cyclical industrial heading into a sudden global shutdown. Even before management formally withdrew guidance on March 23 investors appear to have been pricing in lower equipment demand disrupted dealer activity and much worse visibility.

primary_cause: Crude-price collapse from Saudi-Russia oil war plus COVID demand destruction. Reuters: oil plunged ~25% Mar 9. Chevron later cut 2020 capex by B and suspended buybacks Mar 24
secondary_factors: Anticipation of capex cuts. Buyback suspension. Energy-sector balance-sheet stress
store_description: Chevron drop was fundamentally oil-driven. By March 16 investors were looking at a combined shock of a roughly 25% crude collapse from the price war and a rapidly worsening demand hit from lockdowns and they were right to expect drastic spending cuts.

primary_cause: No stronger Cisco-specific negative filing. Already canceled or altered major events. Enterprise-networking and hardware demand fears in fast-moving recession
secondary_factors: Supply-chain concerns. Multiple compression in large-cap tech
store_description: Cisco move looks more like a macro and sector repricing than a single company event. Investors were likely worried that enterprise and telecom customers would freeze spending while global supply chains and customer engagement channels were being disrupted.

primary_cause: No clearly negative CVS-specific Reuters headline. Aetna said would waive copays for COVID-19 diagnostic testing. Panic selling in managed-care and retail-health names
secondary_factors: General liquidation. Concerns around front-store traffic mix. Healthcare-policy uncertainty. Uncertainty around medical-cost exposure and recession
store_description: No clearly negative CVS-specific Reuters headline in the prior 3 days. The best explanation is that the market was struggling to price the insurance and care-cost implications of the pandemic even as CVS and Aetna took actions like waiving testing copays.

primary_cause: No major GD-specific Mar 13-16 headline. Gulfstream business-jet exposure to travel and corporate-spending collapse. Repricing of Gulfstream and business-jet exposure
secondary_factors: Broad industrial and aerospace de-risking. Cash-raising sell pressure
store_description: This looks more sector-specific than company-specific. Investors were marking down anything tied to aerospace and travel and GD Gulfstream franchise likely drove most of the downside even though the defense side should have been relatively more resilient.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Reuters Mar 17 reported Alameda County said Tesla could not continue to operate Fremont plant normally under Bay Area lockdown. Factory employed 10,000+ workers annualized production slightly above 415,000 vehicles
secondary_factors: Broader auto-demand fears. Uncertainty about what counted as essential business
store_description: This one had a clean stock-specific catalyst. On the drop date itself Reuters reported that county authorities said Tesla main U.S. factory could not keep operating normally under the lockdown putting a more than 415,000-unit annualized production base at risk.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. Mar 7 compensate drivers diagnosed or quarantined up to 14 days. Mar 17 suspended Uber Pool in U.S. and Canada. Mar 13 closed Greenlight Hubs. Rapid collapse in ride demand
secondary_factors: Driver-support costs. Operational disruption. Fear core rides business would deteriorate faster than Eats could offset
store_description: Uber had multiple relevant pandemic headlines but the main issue was simple: mobility demand was evaporating. Suspending Pool and closing support hubs were defensive operational responses while the driver-compensation policy added costs.

primary_cause: COVID-driven airline and aviation collapse layered on 737 MAX crisis. Reuters later reported Boeing suspended dividend and CEO pay Mar 20 in connection with coronavirus-related aid requests
secondary_factors: Liquidity fears. Expected production disruption. Looming need for government support
store_description: Boeing was already weakened by the MAX grounding so the pandemic-driven collapse in global air travel hit an already fragile equity story. Even though the most explicit company actions came a few days later the market was clearly pricing the risk.
